title: Reverse Vowels of a String
description: Brute force to optimized: collecting vowels into a separate list versus a two pointer in place swap.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string s, reverse only the vowels within it, leaving every consonant exactly where it already is.

blocks.text: Given a string s, reverse only the vowels within it, leaving every consonant exactly where it already is.

blocks.title: Analogy: Swapping Only the Vowel Seats on a Bus
blocks.text: Like a bus full of passengers where only the ones labeled as vowels get up and swap seats with each other from opposite ends of the bus, while every consonant passenger stays seated exactly where they started.

blocks.caption: Only the vowels swap positions, every consonant stays exactly where it is

blocks.text: With no vowels present at all, there is nothing to reverse, so the string stays "xyz", unchanged.
It helps to ask whether reversing the vowels really requires pulling them out into their own separate structure first.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Reverse a String already established the two pointer, converge from both ends, swap technique for reversing a sequence entirely in place, with no extra storage needed.

Observation 2: Here, not every position should be swapped, only vowels matter, so that same converging two pointer technique needs one addition: a skip condition that advances past any consonant without touching it.

Observation 3: The left pointer advances forward whenever it currently sits on a consonant, and the right pointer retreats backward whenever it sits on a consonant, so a swap only ever happens once both pointers have independently arrived at a vowel.

Observation 4: Tracing s equal to "leetcode" confirms it, the pointers skip past consonants like the leading l and the trailing d, and swap only the vowel pairs they land on together, converging correctly on "leotcede" with no extra list of collected vowels ever needed.
Recognizing that the standard converge-and-swap reversal only needs a skip condition added for consonants is what removes the need to collect vowels into a separate structure at all.

Collect every vowel found in the string, in order, into a separate list. Reverse that list. Then build a new string by walking through the original string, substituting each vowel position with the next value taken from the reversed vowel list, one at a time, while copying every consonant straight across unchanged.

items: Scan the string once, collecting every vowel found into a list, in order.
Reverse that list of collected vowels.
Scan the string again, and at every vowel position, substitute the next unused value from the reversed list, while every consonant is copied unchanged.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Vowels are collected in their original left to right order first, so reversing that list afterward directly produces the order they should be placed back in.
A separate index tracks which reversed vowel to use next, since vowel positions are encountered in the same relative order during both scans.
Every consonant is copied through unchanged in the second scan, since only vowel positions are ever substituted.

blocks.text: Every consonant stays in its original position and every vowel position receives values in reversed order, so this correctly reverses just the vowels.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), for the two passes over the string.
Space: O(n), for the separate collected vowels list and the new result string.
Limitation: collecting the vowels into their own separate list is unnecessary. The same swapping can be done directly within the string itself using two pointers converging from both ends.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it builds an entirely separate list just to hold the vowels in reversed order, when the string itself already has room to hold every value it needs.

What the two pointer converge and swap technique fixes directly: swapping values found at the two ends and moving inward reverses a sequence with zero extra storage, exactly as it does for reversing a whole string.

What has to change for this problem specifically: a skip condition is needed, since consonants must never move, only vowels should ever be swapped.

The core idea: advance whichever pointer currently sits on a consonant, and only swap, then advance both pointers, once they have both landed on a vowel at the same time.

Use two pointers, one starting at the front of the string and one at the back. Advance the front pointer forward whenever it sits on a consonant, and move the back pointer backward whenever it sits on a consonant. Once both pointers land on vowels, swap them directly, then move both pointers one step further inward, repeating until they cross.
Two pointers converging from both ends, skipping consonants and swapping vowels directly.

blocks.caption: Optimized: two pointers converge from both ends, swapping only when both sit on vowels

blocks.text: This works because the two pointers only ever advance past confirmed consonants and only ever swap when both are confirmed to be sitting on vowels, so every swap correctly exchanges two vowel positions while every consonant is left completely untouched throughout the entire scan.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["One or both pointers currently sit on a consonant","That pointer advances inward by one without any swap","Consonants are never moved from their original position"],["Both pointers currently sit on a vowel","The two characters are swapped, then both pointers move one step further inward","Vowel positions are correctly exchanged from the outside in"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each pointer moves inward at most n times total.
Space: O(n) in Python and Java, to hold a mutable copy of the immutable input string (O(1) extra in C++, where strings are already mutable in place).

blocks.text: The two pointer approach avoids the intermediate list of collected vowels entirely, doing the swap directly within the string itself as the pointers converge, which is the same "converge from both ends" pattern used for reversing an entire string or array.

items: Forgetting that vowel checks must be case insensitive, since both uppercase and lowercase vowels count.
Advancing both pointers on every iteration regardless of whether a swap actually happened, which can skip over valid vowel positions.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A string with no vowels at all","The pointers simply pass through without ever swapping anything."],["A string that is entirely vowels","Reverses completely, identical to a full string reversal."]]}

blocks.text: Mention the language specific nuance around string mutability: some languages need an explicit mutable copy (an array of characters) before this in place swapping technique can be applied at all.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the extra vowel list", think: two pointers converging from both ends, skipping consonants, swapping only vowels.
If the interviewer says "what if the string is immutable in this language", think: copy it into a mutable array of characters first, then apply the same in place technique.
If the interviewer says "what about uppercase vowels", think: check membership against both cases, or normalize case before checking.

items: Why does the skip condition need to check both the left and right pointer's current character before deciding to swap?

How would this approach change if the string could contain other special, non-alphabetic characters that should also stay untouched, like digits or punctuation?
How would you count the total number of swaps performed without changing the final result?
How would you reverse vowels across a sentence made of multiple words, treating word boundaries as fixed points?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space for the separate vowel list and result string. Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) or O(1) extra space depending on whether the language's strings are mutable in place.

items: Pattern: two pointers converging from both ends, skipping consonants and swapping only when both land on vowels.

Core Idea: the standard converge-and-swap reversal technique needs only a skip condition added, advancing past consonants untouched and swapping only genuine vowel pairs, to reverse just the vowels with no extra storage.
Time: O(n) for both the brute force and optimized approaches.
Space: O(n) for the brute force's separate vowel list, O(n) or O(1) for the optimized approach depending on string mutability.

Most Important Observation: a reversal technique built for an entire sequence can be narrowed to only a subset of positions just by adding a skip condition, no fundamentally new technique is required.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once the two pointer reversal pattern is known; remembering the case insensitive vowel check and the skip-then-swap order is what avoids small bugs.
One line memory trick: skip consonants from either side, swap only when both pointers land on vowels.
